extracted.intended_audience: startup founders, inventors, in-house and outside patent counsel, IP managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting patent applications with an investor/portfolio lens — prioritizing claims and portfolio architecture to maximize commercial, licensing, enforcement, and acquisition value rather than mere issuance/compliance. Emphasizes detectability, market scope, family planning, and recordkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat patents as investment assets, not compliance documents
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is a financial asset. Drafting choices should be evaluated by their effect on the asset's value (licensing potential, enforcement potential, defensive value at acquisition). A patent that is 'filed' is not the goal; a patent that creates economic value is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate every drafting decision by its impact on commercial value: will the claim scope enable licensing, enforcement, or add defensive/acquisition value? Avoid drafting solely to satisfy formalities or to 'file something' without regard to market relevance. Prioritize claims and specifications that support monetization and enforceability over procedural completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investor's lens on claim scope (market-driven scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent's value is roughly proportional to the size of the market its claims cover. When choosing claim scope, ask: what is the market my broadest accurate claim reads on?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify the market size your broadest credible claim would cover (e.g., $10M niche vs $1B mass market) and prioritize drafting/scopes that target larger markets when feasible. Balance accuracy and breadth: broader claims that are still accurate and defensible increase portfolio value. Use market knowledge to guide claim breadth choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detectability drives enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that requires reverse-engineering an internal algorithm is hard to enforce. A claim that reads on observable user behavior, network traffic, or physical product features is enforceable without litigation discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make detectability a first-order drafting consideration: draft claims to read on observable artifacts (user actions, logs, network traffic, visible product features). Antipatterns: claims relying on hidden server-side behavior or internal-only steps that are difficult to prove in court. Prefer claim elements that can be proven with external evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: File internal-process patents sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal manufacturing processes, server-side algorithms, and back-office workflows are often poor patent candidates: hard to detect infringement, easy to keep as trade secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider trade secret protection instead of patenting for internal, non-detectable processes. Weigh detectability and enforcement cost against disclosure/term limits of patent protection. Avoid filing patents where infringement is unlikely to be provable or where secrecy is more valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims as marketing for acquirers
rubrics_metrics.description: When a startup is acquired, the acquirer's IP team reviews the portfolio. A portfolio with claims that obviously read on competitors' products, or that obviously cover the company's flagship product, signals quality. A portfolio with vague aspirational claims signals filed-and-forgotten quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims so they clearly map to real products and competitive landscapes; ensure the portfolio tells a coherent story about the company's tech and market position. Antipatterns: vague aspirational claims that don't clearly read on tangible implementations — these reduce perceived acquisition value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't over-index on issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuance is a milestone, not the goal. A patent that issued with overly narrow claims because the applicant gave up early in prosecution is worth less than a pending application with broader claims still being negotiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to appeal, file RCEs, or abandon and refile when issuance would lock in unduly narrow claims. Treat prosecution as part of value-maximization, not merely a compliance box. Antipatterns: conceding overly narrow claim constructions simply to obtain issuance quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: File on the crown jewel first
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the 1-2 features of your product that are (a) hardest for competitors to design around and (b) most central to customer value. File on those first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize filings covering the most defensible and commercially important features. Defensive filings on minor features can wait. Use product and competitive analysis to identify crown-jewel features that will maximize enforcement/licensing value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document the inventive story (secondary considerations file)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond the spec, keep a record of: when the invention was conceived, what prior art the inventor knew of, what alternatives were considered, what failures occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain contemporaneous inventor records and a secondary-considerations file to support non-obviousness (103) and litigation positions. Include dates of conception, known prior art, alternatives evaluated, failed experiments, and motivations. This documentation is useful in prosecution (e.g., rebutting obviousness) and in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent family architecture planning
rubrics_metrics.description: A serious portfolio includes a parent, multiple continuations claiming different scopes, and foreign counterparts. Plan the family architecture at filing, not retroactively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the initial filing stage, map out desired claim-scope diversification via continuations and decide foreign filing strategy. Use continuations to pursue broader or narrower claim sets over time. Plan territorial coverage consistent with target markets and acquisition/licensing goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use maintenance-fee deadlines as portfolio audits
rubrics_metrics.description: The 3.5, 7.5, and 11.5 year maintenance fee deadlines are good times to audit each patent: is it still commercially relevant? does it still cover competitors' products? would a continuation add value?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat maintenance-fee milestones as forced checkpoints to abandon low-value patents, continue valuable ones, or pursue continuations. Conduct commercial relevance reviews at those points and be willing to selectively abandon to conserve resources. Consider whether continuations or re-filing would add strategic value before paying fees.
